name: Nora Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for making the time, Nora. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything here is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Ashby Lane Accountants, a firm of about twenty-five people in the suburbs. My clients are family businesses: three restaurants, a funeral director, a flooring shop and a few landlords. I prepare their accounts and tax returns, and I'm usually the one who explains to the owner why their bank balance doesn't match their profit.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the families. The funeral director, Mr Hale, has run the business with his son for thirty years, and I feel trusted with something important. What wears me out is the restaurants, honestly: cash tips, missing till rolls, staff paid three different ways. I use the AI tool the firm bought now and then, mostly to tidy up letters, once I'd seen others using it without trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a useful tool that got talked up too much. At work I'd say we were right not to rush. I'm not much for posting, but I'd say it to the ladies in the church choir.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm relieved. My husband Luc is an electrician, we've got good savings, and we're planning our first baby in the next year or two. If AI stays small, the biggest change in my life is a baby, not a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Ashby Lane and keep using the AI tool for letters. Luc and I would go ahead with trying for a baby next spring. I'd keep saving about £700 a month for maternity leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and grateful. It's a steady life, and I like it that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything at work that worries you, even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two of the restaurants are struggling, and if they close we lose the fees. But the funeral director isn't going anywhere, and there's always someone needing accounts. It's a normal worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would maternity leave work at the firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They're decent about it. I'd get six months on good pay, then I'd want to go back part-time. The partners have said that's possible.

say: AI was a **useful tool** that got **talked up** too much.
Our firm was **right not to rush** into it.
think: I'm **relieved**, with good savings and a husband in a steady trade.
The biggest change in my life is a **baby**, not a computer.
do: Carry on at **Ashby Lane** using the AI tool for letters.
Try for a **baby** next spring with Luc.
Save about **£700 a month** for maternity leave.
S0.quote: If AI stays small, the biggest change in my life is a baby, not a computer.
fieldNote: Nora's household is **secure**, with savings and her husband's electrician work.
Her existing worry is **struggling restaurant clients**, which she treats as normal.
Her life plans centre on **starting a family**, and work fits around it.

steps.text: Keep preparing accounts for family business clients at Ashby Lane
Start trying for a first baby with Luc next spring
Save £700 a month toward maternity leave

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and the firm should train us properly. To friends I'd say there'll still be work for accountants who know their clients. At church I'd say we need to look after people who lose out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the firm would hire fewer people and expect more from each of us. The checking and returns are what the AI takes, so I'd have to get better at it. A part-time accountant on maternity leave is the easiest person for a firm to quietly stop replacing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once a few colleagues had it working, I'd learn the AI tools properly and use them every day. I'd still try for the baby, because Luc's work is steady. But I'd build up the savings a bit more first, maybe to a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd be watching the partners more closely than before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your baby plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't think so. Family comes first, and Luc's trade is safe for years. I might just not tell the firm until I'd sorted out my new skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Brenda, who does payroll and has done for twenty years. She's lovely but she won't touch a new system. I'd try to help her, like someone helped me.

say: The firm should **train us properly** for a big change.
There'll still be work for accountants who **know their clients**.
think: The firm will **hire fewer people** and expect more from each of us.
Being **part-time** after a baby makes me easier not to replace.
do: Learn the **AI tools** properly once colleagues have them working.
Go ahead with **trying for a baby**.
Build savings up to about **a year** first.
S1.quote: A part-time accountant on maternity leave is the easiest person for a firm to quietly stop replacing.
fieldNote: Nora's own job looks **mostly safe**, but she sees a risk in going **part-time**.
She keeps **family first** and won't delay the baby.
Her steady style shows: she'll learn the tools once **others prove them**.

steps.text: Learn the firm's AI tools once colleagues have them working
Keep trying for a baby and tell the firm later
Build savings up to a full year of costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's far too fast and people will get hurt. At church I'd say we need to look after each other, because the government won't be ready. I'd say families and communities will matter more than ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job's gone by 2028 or soon after. It's all screen work, so there's no extra three years for me. Luc's electrical work is hands-on, so he'd have until about 2031, maybe longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd have the baby sooner, while I still have a job with good maternity pay. I'd save every spare penny, around £1,200 a month, and lean on Luc's income and my parents nearby. After the baby, I'd look for something with people in it, maybe the office at Mr Hale's funeral home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I keep thinking about holding a baby while my job disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why have the baby sooner, not later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if I wait, I might not have a job or maternity pay at all. I'd rather have our first baby while my accounting firm Ashby Lane still pays maternity leave than wait and lose both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From family and church, yes, gladly. My mum would help with childcare. I wouldn't want to rely on benefits if we can manage ourselves.

say: It's **far too fast**, and people will get hurt.
**Families and communities** will matter more than ever.
The **government** won't be ready, so we must look after each other.
think: My job's **gone by 2028**, because it's all screen work.
Luc's **electrical work** is hands-on, so he has until about 2031.
do: Have the **baby sooner**, while maternity pay is still there.
Save about **£1,200 a month** and lean on Luc's income.
Look for work at **Mr Hale's funeral home** after the baby.
feel: **Alarmed** about holding a baby while her **job disappears**.
S2.quote: I'd rather have our first baby while my accounting firm Ashby Lane still pays maternity leave than wait and lose both.
fieldNote: Nora expects to **lose her job** and responds by bringing the baby forward.
The **hands-on timing** gap means Luc's income lasts longer than hers.
She'd lean on **family and church** rather than benefits, fitting her traditional views.

steps.text: Try for a baby now while maternity pay still exists
Save about £1,200 a month from both incomes
Ask her mum to help with childcare
Ask Mr Hale about office work at his funeral home

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning we should take seriously. At work I'd push for clear plans for staff. At church I'd say young people should think about trades and caring work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the same as the fast one, just with time to prepare. I'd be 32 by 2031, with a toddler. Five years is enough for me to have a baby and retrain, but not if I wait for anyone else to go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the AI tools now and use them well, so I'm useful for the next few years. We'd have the baby on our normal plan. In year three I'd start a part-time course in something with people, maybe funeral arranging or practice management.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steadier. I'd have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you usually wait for others to go first. Would you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's my habit, yes. But with a child coming, I'd push myself. I wouldn't want to be the last one at the firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why funeral arranging?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Hale's family are the kindest people I work with. They're always in a room with grieving families, and I can't see people wanting a robot for that. I'd ask him how he got started.

say: Five years is a **warning** we should take seriously.
The firm should give staff **clear plans** now.
Young people should consider **trades and caring work**.
think: It's the **same ending**, just with time to prepare.
I'd need to move **before others**, not wait for them.
do: Learn the **AI tools** now and use them well.
Have the **baby** on the normal plan.
Start a part-time course in **funeral arranging** in year three.
S3.quote: Five years is enough for me to have a baby and retrain, but not if I wait for anyone else to go first.
fieldNote: The extra time lets Nora keep her **family plans** while preparing to move.
She'd push past her habit of **waiting for others**, because of the child.
Her pull toward **funeral work** comes from a client she admires.

steps.text: Learn the firm's AI tools well in the first year
Have the first baby on the planned timeline
Start a part-time funeral arranging course in year three

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to plan properly, so let's not panic. At work I'd say train us and keep us. At church I'd say look after the older ones, because they'll find it hardest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years covers having our children and getting them to school. Like I said with the slower one, my desk job ends, but there's room to switch calmly. By 2036 I'd want to be doing work where people need a person in the room, not a person at a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the AI tools as they spread, go part-time after the first baby and keep my clients. Around year five I'd start retraining, probably in funeral work or practice management. Luc and I would keep saving and pay down the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but at peace with it. There's a plan and there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want more children in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably two, spaced out. With ten years and Luc's steady trade, we could afford it. In the fast version I'd stop at one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you move sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the firm stopped taking on trainees, or if the partners started talking about 'efficiency' every meeting. That'd be the sign.

say: Ten years is time to **plan properly**, so there's no need to panic.
Look after the **older staff**, who'll find it hardest.
think: Ten years covers having our **children** and getting them to school.
By 2036 I want work needing a **person in the room**.
do: Learn **AI tools** as they spread and go part-time after the first baby.
Keep saving and **pay down** the mortgage with Luc.
S4.quote: By 2036 I'd want to be doing work where people need a person in the room, not a person at a screen.
fieldNote: With a decade, Nora expects her **job to end** but on a calm timetable.
More time means **two children** instead of one.
Her signal to move is the firm **stopping trainee** hiring.

steps.text: Learn AI tools as they spread through the firm
Have two children, spaced out, and work part-time
Start retraining in funeral work around year five
Overpay the mortgage with Luc each month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it'd land right when we're starting a family. What would help is employers giving long notice and keeping maternity pay for people who are on leave when cuts come. And support for apprenticeships for adults, so people can learn real trades.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe faith. My church will be where people go when their jobs disappear, and I don't think the church is ready either. We should start talking about it now.

headlineQuote: My church will be where people go when their jobs disappear, and I don't think the church is ready either.
portrait: Nora is a **27-year-old accountant** at a suburban firm serving family businesses.
She's married to Luc, an **electrician**, and they plan their **first baby** soon.
She's **calm** if AI stalls and uneasy under slow change.
Under **AGI by 2028**, she'd have the baby sooner, while maternity pay still exists.
Given time, she'd move toward **funeral work**, leaning on family and church along the way.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it would land as they start a family.
whatWouldHelp: Long **notice** and protected **maternity pay** during cuts.
**Adult apprenticeships** so people can learn real trades.
